paras: The killing of Wright was the fatal shooting of a Black man named Wright by a deputy in Sumter County, South Carolina, on December 30, 1880, while deputies tried to arrest him on a charge of stealing a bale of cotton. A Charleston dispatch said Wright had cut and shot Deputy Sheriff Bateman before he was killed, and a coroner's jury later returned a verdict of "justifiable homicide."

A warrant had been issued for Wright on a charge of stealing a bale of cotton, which a North Carolina paper said belonged to James H. Aycock, formerly of Rockingham, North Carolina. Deputy Sheriff E. H. Bateman of Sumter County, a brother of A. J. Bateman of Rockingham, went to arrest him.

According to a special dispatch to the Charleston News and Courier, Wright resisted, "cut and shot" Bateman, and was then shot and killed by "another deputy sheriff." The Rockingham Spirit, writing from the deputy's home town, gave a different picture of the struggle: Wright struck Bateman on the head with a cooking vessel, knocking him down and breaking the "spider" in pieces. The Spirit added that Wright had a pistol and was trying to use it, and that Peter Mallett, whom it believed to be a native of Fayetteville, North Carolina, shot him through the head at Bateman's request, killing him instantly.

A coroner's jury returned a verdict of "justifiable homicide." No report of any further inquiry or prosecution appears in the coverage, and no account from Wright's side or from other witnesses was printed.

The News and Courier dispatch, dated Charleston, December 30, ran nearly word for word the next day in the Richmond Dispatch, the National Republican of Washington and the New-York Tribune. Their headlines framed the same text differently: the Dispatch wrote "Killed While Resisting Arrest," the Tribune "A NEGRO SHOT BY A DEPUTY SHERIFF," and the National Republican "A South Carolina Murder." The Washington Evening Star, under "KILLED BY AN OFFICER," called Wright "a colored thief" rather than a man charged with theft.

Condensed versions circulated for another week in news roundups, among them the Daily Republican's "Three Murders Yesterday," the Baptist Courier's South Carolina column and the Carbon Advocate of Lehighton, Pennsylvania. The Litchfield Enquirer in Connecticut reduced the story to one line, that a deputy sheriff "killed a negro," and dated it the 20th. The fullest account appeared on January 20, 1881, when the Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic reprinted the Rockingham Spirit's local items, which named the shooter and stressed that he fired only when the deputy asked him to.

The wire reports said Bateman was cut and shot and that his wounds were serious, while the Rockingham Spirit, correcting its own earlier report that he had been shot, said he was struck with a cooking vessel and that his wounds, "though severe, are not serious." The wire also called the shooter a deputy sheriff, whereas the Spirit named him as Peter Mallett without giving him any office.

reader.title: Killing of Wright in Sumter County, South Carolina
bases: Wright was shot dead by a man described as a deputy sheriff while deputies tried to arrest him on a theft warrant; no crowd or mob is reported (A2, A4, A9).

The News and Courier wire dispatch (A2, A3, A4) and the separate Rockingham Spirit account (A9) agree that Wright was shot and killed while resisting arrest on a charge of stealing a bale of cotton, though they differ on details.

accounts.label: News and Courier wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Wright, wanted on a warrant for stealing a bale of cotton, resisted arrest, cut and shot Deputy Sheriff Bateman, and was then shot and killed by another deputy sheriff; Bateman's wounds were serious.

accounts.label: Rockingham Spirit (via Farmer and Mechanic)
accounts.gist: Wright struck Bateman on the head with a cooking 'spider', had a pistol and was trying to use it; Peter Mallett, at Bateman's request, shot him through the head, and a coroner's jury found justifiable homicide.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Charleston dispatch nearly word for word, varying only the headline: 'Killed While Resisting Arrest' (Richmond), 'A NEGRO SHOT BY A DEPUTY SHERIFF' (New York), 'A South Carolina Murder' (Washington).
The Evening Star called Wright 'a colored thief' outright, and the Rockingham Spirit stressed that he had a pistol and that the shooter fired only when asked by the deputy.
Brief roundups placed the killing among the day's murders and casualties without comment.
